strengths: Compelling motivational analysis: The paper provides clear quantitative and qualitative evidence that vision tokens intrinsically encode grounded textual semantics, which are obscured under the full vocabulary but become prominent under context-aware vocabulary constraints.

Efficient training-free formulation: ReVisiT precomputes vision token projections once during the prompt forward pass, requiring no additional multi-pass forward passes during autoregressive generation. As demonstrated, it incurs negligible latency overhead (+0.6% to +1.9% compared to greedy decoding), substantially outperforming previous contrastive decoding baselines in computational efficiency.

Comprehensive empirical validation: The method is evaluated across five diverse benchmarks spanning hallucination detection (CHAIR, POPE, HallusionBench) and general multimodal reasoning (MMMU, VQAv2) across multiple model architectures and scales (LLaVA-1.5, Qwen2.5-VL, InternVL up to 32B), demonstrating consistent gains and generality.
Well-structured ablations: The ablations thoroughly examine the choice of divergence metric, token selection strategy, vocabulary subsetting, layer scopes, and candidate threshold hyperparameter α.
weaknesses: Memory overhead of logit caching: Precomputing and caching the projected vision distribution $l_{\text{vision}} \in \mathbb{R}^{|\mathcal{J}| \times |v| \times |\mathcal{V}|}$ requires storing full vocabulary logits across candidate layers and vision tokens. In modern high-resolution models with large vocabularies (e.g., Qwen2.5-VL with $|\mathcal{V}| \approx 152\text{k}$ and hundreds to thousands of visual tokens), this can introduce non-trivial GPU memory overhead (several gigabytes), which warrants explicit discussion.

Heuristic layer selection across architectures: The choice of candidate layer set $\mathcal{J}$ differs substantially across models (the last decoder layer for LLaVA vs. all even-numbered layers for Qwen2.5-VL). The manuscript lacks a principled rule or automated criterion for how to configure $\mathcal{J}$ when deploying ReVisiT to unseen LVLM architectures.

Fixed unweighted combination: In Eq. (6), the base distribution and selected vision token distribution are combined strictly via equal element-wise multiplication (equivalent to adding unweighted log-probabilities). The paper does not explore whether an adaptive or tuned weight hyperparameter (e.g., $p_{\text{base}} \times p_{\text{ref}}^\beta$) would prevent over-reliance on visual cues at non-visual or syntactic generation steps.

strengths: Compelling motivational analysis: The paper presents insightful empirical and statistical analyses demonstrating that vision tokens encode latent textual semantics through the language modeling head, and that ground-truth objects remain accessible in output distributions during hallucination steps under context-aware vocabulary constraints.

Remarkable computational efficiency: Unlike standard contrastive decoding methods (e.g., VCD, M3ID, SID) that require auxiliary forward passes or input perturbations (incurring ~2x runtime overhead), ReVisiT precomputes vision token projections once at prompt processing and achieves competitive or superior grounding with negligible decoding overhead (+0.6% to +1.9% over greedy decoding).

Comprehensive empirical validation: Evaluated across five diverse benchmarks spanning both hallucination mitigation (CHAIR, POPE, HallusionBench) and general multimodal reasoning/VQA (MMMU, VQAv2), demonstrating consistent improvements across multiple model families (LLaVA-1.5, Qwen2.5-VL, InternVL2.5/3) and parameter scales from 7B to 32B.

Thorough ablation and failure analysis: The paper meticulously ablates key components (vocabulary constraint, divergence selection criteria, layer selection, threshold alpha) and clearly explains why unconstrained full-vocabulary projection fails degenerately.
weaknesses: Heuristic layer selection: The choice of candidate decoder layers J is model-dependent and determined empirically (e.g., only the last layer for LLaVA-1.5 vs. all even layers for Qwen2.5-VL), lacking a unified, automated, or principled selection rule.

Task-dependent tuning of threshold alpha: The APC threshold alpha requires adaptation between generative tasks (larger candidate pool) and discriminative tasks (smaller candidate pool); a fully self-calibrating or dynamic threshold would further strengthen the method's plug-and-play usability.

Rigid logit combination: Equation (6) combines base logits and selected vision token logits with equal weighting (pure multiplication/sum in log-space) without an interpolation weight, which might not be globally optimal across varying question types and visual saliency levels.

strengths: Compelling motivational analysis: Probing vision token representations directly via the LM head (analogous to the logit lens) and observing that latent visual semantics are surfaced when projected over a context-aware constrained vocabulary provides an interesting and well-motivated empirical foundation.

High computational efficiency: Unlike existing contrastive decoding methods (e.g., VCD, M3ID, SID) that require auxiliary forward passes or distorted inputs and introduce roughly 2× latency overhead, ReVisiT precomputes and caches vision token projections once, adding negligible runtime overhead (+0.6% to +1.9%).

Comprehensive empirical validation: The method is extensively evaluated across diverse architectures (LLaVA-1.5, Qwen2.5-VL, InternVL2.5/3), scales (7B to 32B), and benchmark types, spanning both hallucination mitigation (CHAIR, POPE, HallusionBench) and general multimodal reasoning (MMMU, VQAv2).

Thorough ablation study: The paper rigorously validates key design components, notably illustrating why vocabulary constraint is essential (preventing severe degeneration into repetitive strings) and confirming the necessity of context-aware divergence selection.
weaknesses: Potential conceptual tension in token selection: Selecting the vision token via minimum Jensen-Shannon Divergence (min-JSD) with the base LM output distribution means selecting the visual representation that already agrees most with the current text logits. If the model's text prior is dominating towards a hallucination, there is an inherent risk that min-JSD selects a spurious visual token that reinforces this prior rather than correcting it; the paper lacks a formal theoretical explanation or counterfactual analysis of when and why this selection avoids confirmation bias.

Heuristic layer selection and threshold sensitivity: The candidate layer pool differs across model families (e.g., last layer for LLaVA vs. all even layers for Qwen2.5-VL), and the threshold parameter alpha requires tuning across a wide logarithmic range (1e-1 to 1e-6) depending on whether the task is generative or discriminative, which somewhat hinders out-of-the-box generality.

Extreme dependence on the vocabulary subset constraint: As shown in Table 10 and Figure 8, decoding without the adaptive vocabulary constraint causes catastrophic failure (F1 dropping to 1.52 with degenerate repetitive loops). While the authors address this via APC filtering, the fragility of directly combining vision projections without filtering indicates the underlying projection distribution carries significant out-of-distribution noise.

strengths: Novel and conceptually clean approach: ReVisiT cleverly repurposes the vision tokens' representations via a logit-lens projection onto a dynamic vocabulary subset, turning internal visual states into efficient reference signals for decoding without needing extra forward passes.

Outstanding inference efficiency: Unlike existing intra-alignment methods (e.g., VCD, M3ID, SID) that require duplicate forward passes or visual perturbations (incurring ~2x latency), ReVisiT precomputes the vision token projections once during prefill, introducing only a 1-3% latency overhead over greedy decoding.

Extensive empirical validation: The method is evaluated across three prominent hallucination benchmarks (CHAIR, POPE, AMBER) on both dense and MoE architectures (LLaVA-1.5, Qwen2.5-VL, and DeepSeekVL2), consistently outperforming or matching existing baselines while avoiding performance degradation on stronger models.

Insightful ablation and qualitative analysis: The paper clearly demonstrates the necessity of vocabulary truncation/constraint (showing that full-vocabulary projection leads to diffuse noise and severe failure modes) and provides detailed per-token probability shifts in the appendix.
weaknesses: Selection criterion dynamics: The method selects the vision token that minimizes Jensen-Shannon Divergence (JSD) to the base model's constrained distribution. In cases where the base prediction strongly hallucinates towards a distractor, it is not fully analyzed whether minimizing divergence might inadvertently favor a vision token that aligns with the hallucination rather than the true visual ground.

Heuristic logit/probability fusion: The final probability refinement uses unweighted element-wise multiplication ($p_{base} \odot p_{ref}$). The absence of a tunable or adaptive weighting factor between base and reference distributions leaves open questions about balancing visual priors against language coherence across varied prompt types.

Architecture-dependent layer selection: The layer pooling strategy requires distinct configurations across architectures (e.g., final layer only for LLaVA vs. all even-numbered layers for Qwen2.5-VL), indicating that optimal layer selection still relies on empirical heuristics rather than an automated or unified criterion.

strengths: Novel and conceptually clean perspective: The paper introduces ReVisiT, an innovative and elegant intra-alignment decoding method that repurposes the model's internal vision token representations via logit-lens projection to guide visual grounding.

Remarkable computational efficiency: Unlike standard visual contrastive decoding approaches (e.g., VCD, M3ID, SID) that necessitate extra forward passes or perturbed re-evaluations (often incurring ~2x latency), ReVisiT caches vision token projections during the prefill stage and only incurs lightweight vocabulary slicing and divergence computations, resulting in minimal runtime overhead (+2.3% to +3.5% over greedy decoding).

Comprehensive empirical validation: Experiments span multiple standard hallucination benchmarks (CHAIR, POPE across three sub-datasets, and AMBER) across diverse LVLM architectures (LLaVA-1.5, modern Qwen2.5-VL, and MoE-based DeepSeek-VL2), showing consistent improvements over greedy decoding and competitive or superior performance to existing intra-alignment methods.

Insightful analysis and ablations: The ablations convincingly demonstrate why dynamic vocabulary subset constraint is crucial (showing that unconstrained projection leads to catastrophic recall collapse) and provide helpful qualitative and distributional case studies.
weaknesses: Theoretical intuition behind selection objective: The selection mechanism chooses the vision token minimizing Jensen-Shannon Divergence (JSD) with the vanilla output distribution. When the base model's top prediction is already hallucinatory, it is not immediately obvious why minimizing divergence does not simply reinforce the hallucinatory prior. Further theoretical justification or systematic analysis of failure modes where misleading vision tokens are chosen would strengthen the paper.

Model-dependent heuristic choices: Optimal layer pools vary considerably across models (LLaVA-1.5 uses only the last layer, while Qwen2.5-VL requires all even-numbered layers), and the threshold $\alpha$ is tuned differently across generative and discriminative tasks, suggesting sensitivity that may require per-architecture tuning in practical deployment.

Missing evaluation on broader multimodal benchmarks: The evaluation focuses strictly on hallucination and grounding benchmarks (CHAIR, POPE, AMBER). Evaluating whether the proposed decoding strategy preserves general LVLM reasoning capabilities on broad benchmarks (such as MMMU, MMBench, or MathVista) would provide a complete picture of utility.

strengths: High computational efficiency: Unlike prevailing intra-alignment decoding methods (e.g., VCD, M3ID, SID) that require auxiliary forward passes with perturbed inputs or expensive recalibrations, ReVisiT precomputes vision token logit projections during prefill and achieves competitive hallucination reduction with only ~2-3.5% latency overhead.

Sound and comprehensive benchmarking: The method is validated across diverse hallucination benchmarks encompassing both generative captioning (CHAIR, AMBER) and discriminative QA (POPE across COCO, A-OKVQA, and GQA), tested across multiple model families (LLaVA-1.5, Qwen2.5-VL, and DeepSeekVL2 MoE).

Effective empirical improvements over strong baselines: ReVisiT consistently improves over greedy decoding and frequently matches or outperforms 2x-cost contrastive decoding techniques, particularly on challenging adversarial/popular splits on POPE and on CHAIR metrics.

Insightful analysis of the vocabulary constraint: The ablation in Section 4.3 and Appendix C.2 clearly illustrates that unconstrained vision token projections yield severe degeneration and object repetition, justifying the adaptive context-relevant vocabulary subset mechanism.
weaknesses: Heuristic selection and refinement mechanism: The selection criterion chooses the vision token minimizing JSD with the base distribution over the constrained set, followed by element-wise multiplication. When the base model hallucinates with high confidence, the correct token may not be captured in the dynamically constrained candidate set $V_{\text{cons}}^t$, in which case the method cannot recover from the error.

Sensitivity to architecture- and task-specific hyperparameters: The optimal layer selection strategy varies significantly between architectures (e.g., last layer only for LLaVA-1.5 vs. all even layers for Qwen2.5-VL), and the vocabulary cutoff parameter $\alpha$ requires differing choices between generative and discriminative settings, which somewhat limits plug-and-play generality.

Absence of general multimodal capability evaluations: While the paper demonstrates hallucination reduction on CHAIR, POPE, and AMBER, it lacks evaluations on standard broad multimodal benchmarks (e.g., MMBench, MMMU, or ScienceQA) to ensure that the logit refinement does not inadvertently harm complex reasoning or knowledge-intensive tasks.

Modest gains on stronger base models in discriminative settings: On POPE with Qwen2.5-VL (Table 2), the gains over greedy decoding are narrow (84.77% vs. 84.49% accuracy; 83.18 vs. 82.82 F1), showing diminishing returns on more recent architectures.
